newsitem.title: THAILAND: Analysts say rescue of Thai bank is a debacle.
newsitem.headline: Analysts say rescue of Thai bank is a debacle.

text.p: Thai central bank plans to rescue the Bangkok Bank of Commerce (BBC) should return it to profit, but the way the issue has been handled is embarrassing for the regulators, analysts said on Thursday.

The bank was acknowledged to be on the verge of collapse last May, and it was subsequently discovered that the central bank had known about the problems for at least four years but failed to tackle them, they told Reuters.

Plans unveiled this week should see the central Bank of Thailand pay 30 billion baht ($1.2 billion) to BBC in exchange for its 50 billion baht of non-performing loans. The central bank will then pay BBC to help recover the debt.
The loan purchase payment will be made in the form of an eight-year promissory note on which the Bank of Thailand will service the 12.5 percent interest for the first eight years.
The plan modifies Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan's objective, outlined last month, to sell 51 percent of the bank to a single buyer.
"You could interpret the central bank's plans to swallow some of the bad debts as a limited admission that this problem was partly of their own making," said a banking analyst at a regional broker.
"It is not so much what the central bank did, it is what it didn't do that was the problem," said the analyst.

With the mechanics of the latest plan, particularly a possible invitation to state-owned Industrial Finance Corporation of Thailand (IFCT) to manage BBC, already in doubt, the saga is set to continue, industry sources said.
"I think it is unlikely, very unlikely IFCT will be stuck with this, they just can't just stick them with this. What kind of role will IFCT play seems to be in doubt," said the banking analyst.
After subscribing to a series of capital increases, the central bank currently holds 65 percent of the BBC, and will now continue to do so until the bank returns to profit.
The new plan appeared to surprise most members of a state-controlled committee that has run the bank since last May.

"Though there was a feeling over the last few weeks that the original plans weren't going to work out...the committee was never formally told by the Bank of Thailand that this was happening," said one of its members.

A former proposal to sell off BBC to qualified bidders fell through when talks with two finance companies broke down. A negotiator attributed the breakdown to the central bank constantly "changing the goalposts".

Though prospective bidders would be keen to take over the bank's network of more than 150 branches, the loan burden was too much for the firms, leaving the Bank of Thailand to handle the debts, analysts said.
"This is the only way they can really go forward. They have to cleanse the bank of its debts if they want to return to profit and sell it...," said a local research chief.
"We haven't seen the end of this yet, not for months and months. We are still in the negotiating stages," the bank analyst said.
